title: Flexible working, disability and workplace support: who does what
label: 11 November 2026 · Flexible working & disability
summary: Witnesses from Acas, the EHRC, CIPD and IOSH discussed how return-to-office rules and new flexible-working law interact with employers’ duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled staff; the need for clearer guidance, better manager skills and symptoms-aware practice; proposals for a joined-up health-and-work service; problems with awareness and limits in the Access to Work scheme; and the EHRC’s constrained enforcement capacity.

glossary.definition: An independent body providing guidance and mediation on workplace relations and employment law in Great Britain.
Changes an employer must make to remove disadvantages that a disabled worker faces at work.
A government scheme that pays for support and equipment to help disabled people do a job.
UK law that protects people from discrimination, including disability discrimination and duties on employers.
A legal duty for public bodies to consider how policies affect equality when they make decisions and set services.
A pre-tribunal Acas process intended to resolve workplace disputes before they go to employment tribunal.
Clinical and advisory services that help employers manage employees’ health at work and return-to-work plans.

chapters.title: How employers should consider disabled workers when changing location rules
chapters.takeaway: Employers must treat flexible working requests and reasonable adjustments as separate legal routes and consult disabled staff individually.

turns.speaker: Christine Jardine
turns.text: When employers change home or hybrid working rules, what should they do to make sure disabled workers' needs are properly considered?

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: There’s no one-size-fits-all. Employers must meet Equality Act 2010 duties, consult disabled staff, have open individual conversations, avoid assumptions, and provide accessible equipment and communication.

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: They should assess on-site barriers—noise, sensory overload, commuting, and lack of rest spaces—and keep reviewing policies to avoid isolating people or harming progression.

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: From health and safety: do organisational risk assessments and individual risk assessments. Involve occupational health and safety experts and train managers to have confidential, supportive conversations.

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: Acas sees few formal cases, but we often get calls showing confusion: flexible working requests and reasonable adjustments get mixed up. Employers must not treat disability needs simply as a routine flexible working request.

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: If employers treat adjustments as ordinary flexible working and refuse them, sickness and performance can worsen. Managers are worried about fairness and need to justify tailored decisions without disclosing private health details.

turns.speaker: John Kirkpatrick
turns.text: The EHRC agrees: reasonable adjustments apply regardless of where someone works. Public bodies must consider impacts under the Public Sector Equality Duty before changing policies.

chapters.title: A joined-up health and work service: what it would do
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses favour a coordinated local service offering prevention, self-referral, rehab and clear roles across NHS, occupational health and employers—but funding and fragmentation are big barriers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Ruth, you’ve called for a national integrated health and work service—what would it look like and how would a disabled worker use it?

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: It would be a whole-person, joined-up pathway where people can self-refer to coordinated support—GPs, physio, occupational health and occupational safety advice—covering prevention, return-to-work and long-term rehabilitation.

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: Many small firms lack occupational health; a national system would set minimum service standards, reduce fragmentation and ensure employers can access competent, timely support.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who pays for it?

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: Employers still bear duties and costs for prevention and reasonable adjustments, but Government could fund the infrastructure, quality assurance and access for employers who currently lack services.

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: There’s big potential: recent stats show 1.9 million people had work-related ill health last year and about 300,000 people leave employment because of health each year—preventing even some cases would help.

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: There are many employer vanguards and pilots—over 250—so we must evaluate them properly and share learning. Investing in good people management up front prevents problems later.

chapters.title: Access to Work: awareness, coverage and costs
chapters.takeaway: Access to Work helps some disabled people but awareness is low, it covers a small share of workers, and witnesses urge better signposting and employer guidance rather than shifting full costs to firms.

turns.speaker: Kim Leadbeater
turns.text: Access to Work is useful but underused and funding is tight. How should Government balance raising awareness without overwhelming the scheme?

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: Awareness is patchy. We should map the system so employers use existing expertise—HR, health and safety, occupational health—to resolve many issues and funnel only cases that need government support to Access to Work.

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: Access to Work supports only about 1% of working disabled people. It could advise employers on reasonable adjustments more widely, but shifting more costs onto employers now is risky given other rising costs.

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: Acas guidance shows many adjustments are low or no cost. gov.uk currently sends people straight to apply for Access to Work rather than signposting low-cost fixes—better signposting could reduce pressure on the scheme.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: When you say low-cost, what is the typical figure?

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: There’s a myth of a £75 average. We don’t have a reliable national figure—one thing Government could do is establish realistic evidence on typical costs.

turns.speaker: Kim Leadbeater
turns.text: The TUC wants jobseekers told in advance what support they'd get from Access to Work—would that work?

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: Advance information and transparency would help. Employers should say what adaptations they can offer during recruitment and ask applicants about support needs confidentially.

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: Yes—open conversations at interview are useful. But many adjustments can be identified by health and safety and occupational health before escalating to Access to Work.

chapters.title: Reasonable adjustments, disclosure, and workplace conflict
chapters.takeaway: Conflict often arises from how organisations respond to support needs, especially for invisible or fluctuating conditions; managers need training and psychological safety matters for disclosure.

turns.speaker: Dame Nia Griffith
turns.text: How should employers handle conditions that fluctuate, like rheumatic disease, where someone may be fine one day and disabled the next?

turns.speaker: John Kirkpatrick
turns.text: The law covers fluctuating conditions under the Equality Act if they have a substantial long-term effect on day-to-day activities. Reasonable adjustments must be individualised—what’s reasonable varies by person and employer.

turns.speaker: John Kirkpatrick
turns.text: We don’t currently see a need for a separate code like the menopause guidance; existing guidance already addresses fluctuating conditions, though clarity is always useful.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: Acas notes more of its early conciliation cases involve disability discrimination—why?

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: We can’t claim to explain macro labour trends from EC cases, but our surveys show disabled employees report far more workplace conflict—68% versus 44% for non-disabled workers—and problems often stem from how employers respond to requests for support.

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: Common friction points are delays, treating adjustments as temporary or informal, and using absence or performance processes that become punitive instead of supportive.

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: Managers are critical: conflict is less likely if managers respond quickly, consult, consider alternatives and make sustained, agreed adjustments. Many managers fear saying the wrong thing and need skills to create psychological safety.

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: Workplace adjustment passports are good practice: they store agreed needs and help handovers between managers. But passports don’t replace fresh conversations about the new job and context.

turns.speaker: Ruth Wilkinson
turns.text: We support passports in principle. They can fast-track discussions but employers must still assess the role, the environment and confidentiality; passports are enablers, not full solutions.

chapters.title: Guidance, enforcement and practical next steps
chapters.takeaway: Acas will clarify interactions between flexible-working law and reasonable adjustments in its new code; the EHRC says it would like to do more enforcement and update its guidance but is limited by budget and must be strategic.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How will Acas make sure the new statutory flexible working code doesn’t blur the legal difference with reasonable adjustments?

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: We will keep the legal distinction clear, prompt employers to check whether a request is a flexible working request or a reasonable adjustment, and include equality safeguards: meaningful consultation, accessible processes, privacy and clear reasons for decisions.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The EHRC code on employment is from 2011. Will you update it and clarify flexible working as a potential reasonable adjustment?

turns.speaker: John Kirkpatrick
turns.text: We know the employment code is dated. Updating a statutory code is complex and resource-heavy. We will consider whether targeted guidance or a refresh is needed and would want any new guidance to make clear that flexible working can be a reasonable adjustment.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should the EHRC take a tougher enforcement approach on reasonable adjustments?

turns.speaker: John Kirkpatrick
turns.text: We’d like to do more, but our real-terms budget hasn’t risen for a decade, so our discretionary enforcement funds are limited. We try to be strategic: intervene in high-impact cases, run targeted legal support funds and publish guidance, but more funding would let us do more.

turns.speaker: Claire McCartney
turns.text: From the CIPD viewpoint, give employers more practical support, especially SMEs who are time- and resource-poor. We’ve called for more Acas funding so employers can get the help they need rather than just naming and shaming.

turns.speaker: Julie Dennis
turns.text: Acas is shifting to prevention and education. Getting managers the skills to have everyday supportive conversations should reduce disputes and early conciliation cases.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The Committee will look at these recommendations: better guidance, manager training, joined-up health and work services, clearer Access to Work signposting, and consideration of EHRC resources.
